question: The ongoing ban on the Communist Party of Poland raises serious questions in relation to the respect of fundamental democratic freedoms and civil rights in the European Union. According to public information, proceedings have been brought before the Constitutional Tribunal of Poland at the request of the country’s President, with a view to the party’s removal from the register of political parties.

This development comes on top of the longstanding legal and political pressure faced by the Communist Party of Poland. It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of freedom of thought, conscience and political expression, as well as in relation to the pluralism and democratic functioning of political systems in the Member States.

At the same time, there is the broader question of finding the right balance between the national legal order and the obligations stemming from the European acquis and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. How does the Commission assess these developments in the context of protecting democratic freedoms and freedom of thought and conscience?
What measures does it intend to take, within the remit of its competences, to ensure respect for fundamental rights and political pluralism in Poland and more widely across the European Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) The Commission is aware of the December 2025 ruling from Poland's Constitutional Tribunal banning the Communist Party of Poland.

The Commission is committed to protect and promote EU values and fundamental rights enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (‘the Charter’), including its Article 10 on the right to freedom of thought and conscience, within the remit of its competences.

According to its Article 51 (1), the Charter applies to EU bodies or to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. Based on the information available, it does not appear that the matter raised by the Honourable Member is linked to the implementation of EU law. The Commission has no general powers to intervene in the registration of national political parties and national electoral matters.
It is for the national competent authorities in each Member State to follow up on matters relating to the applicable regulations.
